messages.content: Could you make this more polite? Move your bag. I need that seat, and I have been standing for an hour.
Excuse me, could you please move your bag? I would like to sit down, as I have been standing for an hour. Thank you.
Change this to the future tense: Yesterday we visited the museum, and Asha drew the old coins while I read the labels. Then we ate lunch in the garden.
Tomorrow we will visit the museum, and Asha will draw the old coins while I read the labels. Then we will eat lunch in the garden.

Modern English, please, for these lines.

Then Bharat for the road prepared,
And with Satrughna forth he fared.
First to his sire he bade adieu,
Brave Rama, and his mothers too.
Lord Yudhajit with joyful pride
Went forth, the brothers by his side,
And reached the city where he dwelt:
And mighty joy his father felt.

Then Bharat got ready for the journey, and he set out with Satrughna. First he said goodbye to his father, to brave Rama, and to his mothers. Lord Yudhajit proudly went out with the two brothers at his side. They reached the city where he lived, and his father was overjoyed.
Write this as a short text message to Nisha: Tell Nisha that football practice has been moved from Thursday to Friday and that she should bring her own water bottle and her boots.
Hi Nisha, football practice is now on Friday, not Thursday. Please bring your own water bottle and your boots.
Rewrite this for a young child: Please do not run near the swimming pool, as the tiles are slippery and you could fall and hurt yourself.
Do not run near the pool. The tiles are slippery. You could fall and hurt yourself.

Make this shorter, in two sentences.

Yogesh, nearly two, had opened every kitchen drawer in the flat. He licked a spoon and tore the pages off an old calendar. On the balcony he stuffed a tulsi leaf into his mouth and made a face. His father, Mridul, had stopped saying "No!" every minute. Instead he had tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high, and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons, just for Yogesh.

Nearly two, Yogesh opened every kitchen drawer in the flat, licking a spoon, tearing an old calendar and tasting a tulsi leaf. His father, Mridul, stopped saying "No!" all day and instead tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons for Yogesh.

Rewrite this Panchatantra passage for a young child, in short sentences.

In a certain pond lived two fishes whose names were Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit. And a frog named Single-Wit made friends with them. Thus all three would for some time enjoy at the water's edge the pleasure of conversation spiced with witticisms, then would dive into the water again. One day at sunset they were engaged in conversation, when fishermen with nets came there, who said to one another on seeing the pond: "Look! This pond appears to contain plenty of fish, and the water seems shallow. We will return at dawn." With this they went home.

In a pond lived two fish, Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit. A frog called Single-Wit became their friend. The three of them often chatted and joked at the edge of the water. Then they dived back in. One evening at sunset, some fishermen came with nets. They looked at the pond. "This pond has plenty of fish," they said to each other. "The water looks shallow too. We will come back at dawn." Then they went home.
Put this in the past tense: I wake up at six, make tea for Papa, and walk to the bus stop with Rohan. We talk about cricket until the bus comes.
I woke up at six, made tea for Papa, and walked to the bus stop with Rohan. We talked about cricket until the bus came.

What do these lines say in everyday English? Please answer in prose.

That night Trisanku underwent
Sad change in shape and lineament.
Next morn, an outcast swart of hue,
His dusky cloth he round him drew.
His hair had fallen from his head,
And roughness o'er his skin was spread.
Such wreaths adorned him as are found
To flourish on the funeral ground.
Each armlet was an iron ring:
Such was the figure of the king,
That every counsellor and peer,
And following townsman, fled in fear.

That night Trisanku's body changed. By morning he was an outcast with dark skin, wearing a dusky cloth. His hair had fallen out and his skin was rough. He wore garlands like those found in a funeral ground, and his armlets were iron rings. He looked so frightening that every counsellor, noble and townsman who followed him ran away in fear.
Shorten this note for the fridge door: Please remember that tomorrow is the last day to hand in the form and the money for the school trip, so do not forget it in the morning.
Tomorrow is the last day to hand in the school trip form and money. Don't forget!
Make this letter opening friendlier: Dear Aunt Shobha, I trust that this letter finds you in good health and good spirits.
Hi Aunty Shobha, I hope you're doing well and feeling cheerful!

Shorten this to under 50 words.

In Class 5, the teacher held a riddle contest. 'What has keys but can't open locks?' Devika's hand shot up. 'A piano!' Omkar muttered, 'Oh, look, our genius.' Devika turned around sharply, then saw him smiling and giving a thumbs up. She grinned and whispered, 'Jealous?' He laughed. Next riddle, Omkar got it right. Devika clapped and said, 'Look who's awake today!' They both burst out laughing, and the teacher shook her head, smiling.

In Class 5, Devika won the first riddle with the answer "a piano". Omkar teased her, but his smile and thumbs up showed he was friendly. When he solved the next one, she teased him back. They laughed together while the teacher shook her head, smiling.

Make this more formal, as if for a note to the residents' committee.

I'm Nandini from the flat downstairs. This morning I watched little Sunaina, who is two, stop dead in the parking area. She pointed at the back of a white car and shouted, "Uncle face!" Two red lights, a bumper like a moustache. She laughed so hard she sat down. Then she found another face on a scooter. I can't say what she saw, exactly. But she looked thrilled.

I am Nandini, a resident of the flat downstairs. This morning I observed Sunaina, a child of about two, stop abruptly in the parking area. She pointed to the rear of a white car and called out, "Uncle face!" The car had two red lights and a bumper resembling a moustache. She laughed so hard that she sat down, and then she found another face on a scooter. I cannot say exactly what she saw, but she appeared delighted.

Retell this for a small child, in very simple sentences.

First week of monsoon term: Jahnavi, five, shouts answers, won't sit in the circle, and throws her crayons when told to wait. Jagdish Sir stays calm.

Third week: she sits in the circle but calls out once. Jagdish Sir says, "Hand up, please," and she slowly raises it.

Sixth week: she raises her hand, waits for her turn, and gives her answer. She smiles.

In the first week of the rains, Jahnavi was five and very loud. She shouted answers. She would not sit in the circle. When she had to wait, she threw her crayons. Jagdish Sir stayed calm.

In the third week, she sat in the circle. She still called out once. Jagdish Sir said, "Hand up, please." Slowly, she raised her hand.

In the sixth week, she raised her hand and waited for her turn. Then she gave her answer. She smiled.

Put this Panchatantra passage into plain modern English.

In the southern country was a city called Maidens' Delight. It rivaled the city of heaven's King, so abounding in every urban excellence as to form the central jewel of Earth's diadem. Its contour was like that of Kailasa Peak.

In the south there was a city called Maidens' Delight. It was as grand as the city of Indra, king of heaven, and so full of everything a good city should have that it was the central jewel in the crown of the Earth. Its shape was like the peak of Mount Kailasa.
Turn this into the active voice: A letter was sent to every parent by the school, and a reply was requested by the principal before Monday.
The school sent a letter to every parent, and the principal requested a reply before Monday.

Please make this a formal incident note, in the third person.

At playgroup I saw Gautam, two, reach for the yellow ball in Nikita's hands and then shove her. She sat down hard and cried. The teacher stepped in calmly, picked up Nikita first and checked her knees. Then she crouched by Gautam. "You wanted that ball so much. Pushing hurts. You can say, 'Mine!' or 'My turn!'" Gautam shouted "Mine!" looking at the ball. I can't be sure what he felt, but his fists stayed tight for a while.

Observation, playgroup: Gautam, aged two, reached for a yellow ball held by Nikita and pushed her. Nikita sat down hard and cried. The teacher intervened calmly, lifted Nikita first and checked her knees. She then crouched beside Gautam and told him that he had wanted the ball very much, that pushing hurts, and that he could say "Mine!" or "My turn!" Gautam shouted "Mine!" while looking at the ball. The observer cannot be sure what he felt, but his fists stayed tight for a while.

I'd like this retold for a very young child, like a gentle bedtime story.

Vikas, five, went to the temple fair with his Masi, Sunaina. He rode the small wheel and got a red balloon.
At home he told Dadi, "I rode the big wheel!" The next day he told his friend, "I rode the big wheel, and it went up to the clouds." That evening, after hearing a story about a flying horse, he added, "A horse flew past me!"
Sunaina smiled. "Tell me about your balloon," she said.
Vikas held up the string proudly.

Vikas was five. He went to the temple fair with his Masi, Sunaina. He rode the small wheel. He got a red balloon. At home he told Dadi, "I rode the big wheel!" The next day he told his friend that the wheel went up to the clouds. That evening he heard a story about a flying horse. Then he said that a horse flew past him! Masi Sunaina smiled. She said, "Tell me about your balloon." Vikas held up the string. He was very proud.
I need a casual version for the class chat: We regret to inform you that the picnic scheduled for Sunday has been cancelled due to rain.
Sorry, everyone, the Sunday picnic is cancelled because of the rain.

Rewrite in the first person. The writer is Saanvi.

Saanvi finished her essay late and handed it in with an apology. Her teacher accepted it but asked her to start earlier next time.
I finished my essay late and handed it in with an apology. My teacher accepted it but asked me to start earlier next time.

Shorten this to four sentences, keeping it in the first person.

I'm Jomon, Farida's neighbour. During Ramzan I often go over at sunset. Yesterday her Nani put out jalebis and told Farida, "One now, or three after we break the fast." Farida stared at the plate. Then she sat on her hands, turned her back to it and started singing loudly. Her cousin Sameer ate one and waved it at her. She shut her eyes. When the call to prayer sounded and everyone broke the fast, she got her three. I don't know how she did it; I'd have grabbed one.

During Ramzan I often visit my neighbour Farida at sunset. Yesterday her Nani offered her one jalebi now or three after the fast. Farida sat on her hands and sang loudly to resist, even when her cousin Sameer waved a jalebi at her, and she got her three when everyone broke the fast. I would have grabbed one.
Make this thank-you note sound more formal: Thanks a lot for helping with the project, it was super, and the team really liked your ideas.
Thank you very much for your help with the project. It was greatly appreciated, and the team valued your ideas.

Put this verse into plain modern English.

As rules prescribe the hermit took
Some lustral water from the brook.
But still on this his constant thought
Kept brooding, as his home he sought;
While Bharadvaja paced behind,
A pupil sage of lowly mind,
And in his hand a pitcher bore
With pure fresh water brimming o'er.
Soon as they reached their calm retreat
The holy hermit took his seat;
His mind from worldly cares recalled,
And mused in deepest thought enthralled.

Following the rules, the hermit took some holy water from the brook. But his mind stayed on one thought as he walked home. Behind him walked Bharadvaja, a humble pupil sage, carrying a pitcher filled to the brim with fresh water. When they reached their quiet hermitage, the holy man sat down. He turned his mind away from worldly cares and sat thinking deeply.

Rewrite this as a diary entry in Minakshi's own voice, in the first person.

The rain was coming down hard, and the power had gone. Minakshi's floor was covered with toys, and Aai had said tidy before the lamp was lit. Minakshi stood in the doorway. Everywhere she looked there was something. She sat down in the middle, picked up a doll and began to brush its hair. When her brother Harish came with the lamp, nothing was put away.

The rain was coming down hard, and the power had gone. My floor was covered with toys, and Aai had said to tidy up before the lamp was lit. I stood in the doorway. Everywhere I looked there was something. So I sat down in the middle, picked up a doll and began to brush its hair. When my brother Harish came with the lamp, nothing was put away.

Turn this conversation into a short paragraph of narration, with no quotation marks.

"Joseph, stop running!" the teacher called.

Joseph, six, stopped. "But Vijay was running too!"

"Joseph, don't argue."

Joseph folded his arms and sat on the bench, glaring. He wanted to say, "You're mean!"

At snack time, his friend Vijay came over. "Sorry. I ran too."

Joseph went to the teacher. "Can I tell you something?"

"Of course."

"Vijay was running too. I felt it was unfair."

"Thank you for telling me calmly. You're right. I'll remind both of you."

The teacher called out to Joseph to stop running. Joseph, six, stopped and said that Vijay had been running too. The teacher told him not to argue. Joseph folded his arms and sat on the bench, glaring. He wanted to say that she was mean. At snack time, his friend Vijay came over and said sorry for running too. Joseph went to the teacher and asked if he could tell her something. She said of course. He told her that Vijay had been running too and that it had felt unfair. She thanked him for telling her calmly, said he was right, and promised to remind both boys.

Rewrite in the third person. The speaker is Ananya.

I forgot my tiffin at home, so I shared Deepak's lunch. I promised him I would bring sweets for him tomorrow, and he laughed and said I did not have to.
Ananya forgot her tiffin at home, so she shared Deepak's lunch. She promised him she would bring sweets for him tomorrow, and he laughed and said she did not have to.
Rewrite this for the school office in a formal style: Sir, my son has fever so he will not come tomorrow, he will come after he is fine. Please excuse him.
Respected Sir, my son has a fever and will not be able to attend school tomorrow. He will return once he has recovered. I request you to kindly excuse his absence.
Put this into reported speech: Dad said to me, "I will pick you up at five, so please wait at the gate."
Dad told me that he would pick me up at five and asked me to wait at the gate.

Could you rewrite this old verse as short, simple sentences for a child?

He spoke; and at the monarch's call
The best of hermits told him all,
How in the grove with him they dwelt,
And slaughter to the demons dealt.
Then wonder filled the monarch's breast,
Who tended well each royal guest.
Thus entertained, the princely pair
Remained that night and rested there,
And with the morn's returning ray
To Mithila pursued their way.

The king spoke, and at his request the best of the hermits told him everything. They told how they had lived together in the grove, and how the demons had been killed there. The king was amazed. He looked after each royal guest well. The two princes spent the night resting there. At dawn the next morning they set off for Mithila.
Turn this into a polite request for my neighbour: Stop playing loud music at night. I can't sleep and I have an exam.
Hello, I'm sorry to trouble you, but I have an exam and the loud music at night is stopping me from sleeping. Could you please turn it down? Thank you so much.
Make this invitation casual and warm: Would you care to join us for dinner at our residence this evening at eight o'clock? Kindly confirm your attendance.
Want to come over for dinner tonight at eight? Tell me if you can make it!
Make this more polite for a receptionist to say to a visitor: Tell me your name and number. Then sit there and wait.
May I have your name and number, please? Then please take a seat and wait here.

Rewrite these lines from the Ramayana as simple prose for a school child.

Thus did the king the kings exhort:
They heard, and turned them from the court
And, each to each in friendship bound,
Went forth to all the realms around.
The rites were o'er, the guests were sped:
The train the best of Brahmans led,
In which the king with joyful soul,
With his dear wives, and with the whole
Of his imperial host and train
Of cars and servants turned again,
And, as a monarch dear to fame,
Within his royal city came.

The king spoke these words to the other kings. They listened and left the court, and each went back to his own land, bound to the others in friendship. The ceremonies were over and the guests had gone. The king, with the best of the Brahmans leading the way, returned happily with his dear wives, his whole army, and his chariots and servants, and entered his royal city.
Make this text to my friend more casual: I would be grateful if you could return the novel I lent you at your earliest convenience, as my sister now wishes to read it.
Hey, could you give me my novel back when you get a chance? My sister wants to read it now.

Please turn this into reported speech, with no quotation marks.

On Tuesday Saurabh, five, yelled at a boy who bumped his blocks, "You're mean! It's your fault!" On Thursday he did it again. Sonali Ma'am knelt beside him. "Tell me what happened and what you wanted." "He knocked it and I wanted to finish." "Try saying, I was building, please be careful." On the next Monday a boy walked near the tower and Saurabh said, "I was building! Please go round!" and kept stacking.

On Tuesday, five-year-old Saurabh yelled at a boy who had bumped his blocks. He said that the boy was mean and that it was his fault. On Thursday he did it again. Sonali Ma'am knelt beside him and asked him to tell her what had happened and what he had wanted. He said that the boy had knocked it and he had wanted to finish. She suggested that he say that he was building and that the boy should please be careful. On the next Monday, a boy walked near the tower. Saurabh told him that he was building and asked him to go round, and he kept stacking.

Turn this note into a friendly text message from the teacher.

Note for Harsha's parents
Today we had a birthday in class with a loud music box and balloons. Harsha covered her ears and went to the book corner. She wasn't sulking; she needed quiet. After a while she came back and ate cake with us. At circle time she noticed I'd changed my earrings and that the fish-tank light was dimmer. She also asked, 'Where do people go when they die?' I told her it's a big question and she can ask you too. She's a deep thinker and needs time to warm up.
Mehak

Hi, a quick update on Harsha. The birthday in class was loud, with a music box and balloons, so she covered her ears and sat in the book corner for a while. She wasn't sulking, she just needed quiet. She came back and had cake with us. At circle time she noticed my new earrings and the dimmer fish-tank light, and asked where people go when they die. I said it's a big question and she can ask you too. She's a deep thinker who needs time to warm up. Mehak
Simplify this railway announcement: Passengers are requested to alight only after the train has come to a complete halt and to mind the gap between the train and the platform.
Please wait until the train has fully stopped before you get off. Watch out for the gap between the train and the platform.

Say this in two sentences of modern English.

Then, thus addressed, the holy man,
The very glorious sage, began
The high preliminary rite.
Restraining sense and appetite.
Calmly the youths that night reposed,
And rose when morn her light disclosed,
Their morning worship paid, and took
Of lustral water from the brook.
Thus purified they breathed the prayer,
Then greeted Visvamitra where
As celebrant he sate beside
The flame with sacred oil supplied.

Told to begin, the holy sage started the sacred ceremony, keeping his senses and appetite under control. The young princes rested calmly that night, and at dawn they said their morning prayers, took water from the brook, and greeted Visvamitra, who sat beside the sacred fire fed with holy oil.
Rewrite in the active voice: The windows were cleaned by the children before the guests arrived. The sweets were arranged by Nani, and the lamps were lit by Grandpa.
The children cleaned the windows before the guests arrived. Nani arranged the sweets, and Grandpa lit the lamps.
Please make this email to my professor more formal: Hi Ma'am, can u give me some more time for the assignment? I'm stuck on the last part and my laptop also broke.

Dear Ma'am, I would be grateful if you could give me a little more time to submit my assignment. I am finding the last part difficult, and my laptop has also stopped working. Thank you for your understanding.
Change to the past continuous: Rahul learns to ride a cycle while his father runs behind him. The neighbours watch and clap.
Rahul was learning to ride a cycle while his father was running behind him. The neighbours were watching and clapping.

Change the verbs to the present tense.

At the kerb outside the bakery in Buenos Aires, Liam held out his hand. "Hand, Santiago. Cars." Santiago, two, wanted to run after a pigeon, and for a moment he pulled away. Liam didn't raise his voice; he just waited with his hand out. Santiago looked at the cars, then at his father, and put his small hand in Liam's. On the other side he let go, hugged Liam's leg, and ran to the pigeon.

At the kerb outside the bakery in Buenos Aires, Liam holds out his hand. "Hand, Santiago. Cars." Santiago, two, wants to run after a pigeon, and for a moment he pulls away. Liam doesn't raise his voice; he just waits with his hand out. Santiago looks at the cars, then at his father, and puts his small hand in Liam's. On the other side he lets go, hugs Liam's leg, and runs to the pigeon.

Make this simpler, with short sentences, for a young reader.

At the picnic in a Buenos Aires park, Pablo, five, kicked the ball at his friend Jamal and accidentally hit the water bottle, which rolled into the pond. "Oops!" Pablo clapped his hand over his mouth, wide-eyed. Jamal's shoulders shook. Then his hand flew up over his own mouth, and the two of them dissolved into giggles behind their fingers. Pablo's mother, standing beside the blanket, smiled at them, and Pablo peeked at her face, then lowered his hand.

Pablo was five. He was at a picnic in a park in Buenos Aires. He kicked the ball at his friend Jamal. It hit the water bottle by mistake, and the bottle rolled into the pond. "Oops!" said Pablo. He covered his mouth with his hand. His eyes were wide. Jamal's shoulders shook. Then Jamal covered his own mouth. The two boys giggled behind their fingers. Pablo's mother stood by the blanket and smiled. Pablo peeked at her face. Then he lowered his hand.

Rewrite this in the third person, about Hansa.

I am Hansa, and I live next door to Arohi, who is about two. This morning she sat on our shared landing with her blocks, humming a wordless up-and-down tune. Each time she stacked a block, the hum climbed higher. I hummed back, and she glanced up, grinned and hummed louder. I cannot say why she does it. She looked content to me, though it may just be a tune she picked up somewhere.

Hansa lives next door to Arohi, who is about two. This morning Arohi sat on the shared landing with her blocks, humming a wordless up-and-down tune. Each time she stacked a block, the hum climbed higher. Hansa hummed back, and Arohi glanced up, grinned and hummed louder. Hansa cannot say why she does it. Arohi looked content to her, though it may just be a tune she picked up somewhere.

Put this passage into the present tense.

After her injection at the Bergen clinic, Ingrid screamed. Freya held her against her chest, rocking slowly, and spoke in a low, slow voice. "I know. That hurt. I'm here." Ingrid's screams turned to sobs, then hiccups.
Then the nurse briskly lifted Ingrid's arm to put on a plaster. Ingrid stiffened and started screaming again.
Freya began again, low and slow, rocking. Gradually Ingrid quietened.

After her injection at the Bergen clinic, Ingrid screams. Freya holds her against her chest, rocking slowly, and speaks in a low, slow voice. "I know. That hurt. I'm here." Ingrid's screams turn to sobs, then hiccups.
Then the nurse briskly lifts Ingrid's arm to put on a plaster. Ingrid stiffens and starts screaming again.
Freya begins again, low and slow, rocking. Gradually Ingrid quietens.
Change this into reported speech: Meena asked Vikram, "Where did you keep my umbrella, and why is it wet?"
Meena asked Vikram where he had kept her umbrella and why it was wet.
Say this in simpler words: Owing to inclement weather conditions, the outdoor assembly has been postponed until further notice.
The assembly outside has been put off because of bad weather. We will tell you the new date later.
Cut this down to one short sentence: I just wanted to quickly let you know that the meeting which was planned for three o'clock this afternoon has now been shifted to four o'clock instead.
The three o'clock meeting has been moved to four o'clock.

Give me this verse as plain prose in today's English.

Sumantra, ere the word was given,
His chariot from the court had driven,
And Rama, best of all who ride
In cars, came sitting by his side.
The lords of men had hastened forth
From east and west and south and north,
Aryan and stranger, those who dwell
In the wild wood and on the fell,
And as the Gods to Indra, they
Showed honour to the king that day.

Before the order was given, Sumantra had already driven his chariot out of the court. Rama, the best of chariot riders, came and sat beside him. Rulers had hurried there from east, west, south and north, both Aryans and strangers, and people who live in the wild woods and on the hills. As the gods show honour to Indra, they honoured the king that day.

Retell this scene using reported speech instead of dialogue.

"You broke my kite!" Nitin shouted on the Sankranti terrace.
Siddharth, five, looked at the torn paper. "I didn't mean to."
"But you did!"
Siddharth's lip wobbled. Their grandfather said, "What can you do now?"
Siddharth thought. "Say sorry?"
"And?"
"Fix it?"
He found tape and held the paper while Grandpa stuck it. "Sorry, Nitin."
Nitin sniffed. "Okay. You can fly it with me."

On the Sankranti terrace, Nitin shouted that Siddharth had broken his kite. Siddharth, five, looked at the torn paper and said he had not meant to. Nitin said that he had done it anyway. Siddharth's lip wobbled. Their grandfather asked what he could do now. Siddharth thought and suggested saying sorry. His grandfather asked what else. Siddharth said he could fix it. He found tape and held the paper while Grandpa stuck it. Then he said sorry to Nitin. Nitin sniffed and said okay, and told him he could fly it with him.
Explain this to a four-year-old, please: The moon looks different each night because we see different amounts of its sunlit side.
The moon looks different on different nights. The sun shines on one half of the moon. Each night we can see a little more or a little less of that bright half.
Please make this feedback to my friend more encouraging: Your drawing is okay but the colours are dull and the faces look odd.
Your drawing is a good start. Try some brighter colours, and take a little more time on the faces. Keep going!

Two sentences at most, please. Cut this down.

In their third-floor flat in Pune, Lalit woke from his nap and called, "Mumma!" From the kitchen came, "Coming, Lalit! Two minutes." He sat up on the bed with his thumb in his mouth and waited, not crying. His cousin Raghav, visiting for the day, peeped in. "He's not even scared," Raghav said. Mumma came, lifted Lalit and gave him water. Lalit tucked his head under her chin, then wriggled down to show Raghav his truck.

Lalit woke from his nap in their Pune flat and called for Mumma, then waited quietly with his thumb in his mouth while his cousin Raghav remarked that he was not even scared. When Mumma came, gave him water and lifted him, he tucked his head under her chin and then wriggled down to show Raghav his truck.

This is from the Panchatantra, and "it" means a town. Rewrite it in plain, shorter modern English.

In it lived two friends, a weaver and a carpenter. Since they were past masters in their respective crafts, they had earned enough money by their labors so that they kept no account of receipt and expenditure. They wore soft, gaily colored, expensive garments, adorned themselves with flowers and betelleaves, and diffused odors of camphor, aloes, and musk.

In that town lived two friends, a weaver and a carpenter. They were skilled at their crafts and earned enough that they did not bother counting what came in or went out. They wore soft, bright, expensive clothes, decorated themselves with flowers and betel leaves, and smelled of camphor, aloes and musk.

Retell this as one paragraph in the past tense, with no quotation marks.

"Kamal, it's your turn to be the ghost!"
"Wooooo!" Kamal flapped a bedsheet over his head, and all the cousins shrieked and ran across the courtyard.
"Again! Again!"
Kamal laughed so much his tummy hurt. Then he saw Bidisha by the pillar, not running.
"Bidisha, why aren't you playing?"
"It's too loud."
Their Pishi was stringing lights nearby. "Bidisha, would you like to be the ghost's helper? You can hold the torch."
Bidisha thought, then took it. When she shone it on Kamal, everyone screamed with laughter, and Bidisha giggled too.

Kamal was told it was his turn to be the ghost. He flapped a bedsheet over his head and went woooo, and all the cousins shrieked and ran across the courtyard. They begged for more. Kamal laughed until his tummy hurt. Then he saw Bidisha standing by the pillar, not running, and asked why she wasn't playing. She said it was too loud. Their Pishi, who was stringing lights nearby, asked if she would like to be the ghost's helper and hold the torch. Bidisha thought, then took it. When she shone it on Kamal, everyone screamed with laughter, and Bidisha giggled too.
Convert this into the active voice, please: The match was delayed by the rain, and the trophy was handed to the winners by the principal.
The rain delayed the match, and the principal handed the trophy to the winners.
Rewrite using "going to": Neel plays the guitar at the school show. His friends sing along, and the whole class claps.
